A strong start with del Toro’s typical flair for immersive visual style and deep film knowledge (Cameraman’s Revenge, anyone?). But the dream doesn’t last long. The story is bloated, yet still manages to deprive us. In many ways a trial run for Frankenstein. Mainly, the film is an object lesson on anti-fascism with dialogue to make one cringe.  Fine and unfortunately necessary. But the dregs of the film are its painful, pulseless, wooden songs. As the it drags on, the visuals breakdown, rendering the stop-motion puppets coarsely plastic and the superimposed digital effects jarringly non-diegetic. It’s a fine kids movie if you don’t take issue with alcohol, tobacco, blood and graphic on-screen death.

A wonderfully ingenious and aesthetically appealing display of stop-motion animation — and, to me, little else. Guillermo del Toro ’s Pinocchio strikes me as a frustrating waste of technical prowess — namely, the visual presentation and impeccable animation work — with such tepid, handholding material beneath the charming carapace. While worthy and multifaceted topics are indeed tackled, they are done so with no novelty whatsoever (beyond the aesthetic) and mostly with the depth of an entirely unremarkable children’s story. The subject of death is handled somewhat better by the end, but at that stage the damage was all done. With a slew of obnoxiously obvious allegories and a cartoonish simulacrum of fascism, the film attempts to juggle far too much for its feebly thin central storyline to handle; and these characters are so numbingly banal and paper-thin, I couldn’t care enough to get invested in them. Pinocchio himself is an obnoxious embodiment of the ‘innocent outsider can’t comprehend evil’ trope, which is neither new nor interesting when this barebones, and his relationship with Geppetto is as uninspired and one-dimensional. The Cricket is a perplexingly unimportant piece of the puzzle, and when he’s not around it’s easy to forget he is even in the film — and as a narrator, he serves no purpose; most of the time, he simply explains the obvious. As a comic-relief, he is simply irritating. Performances are also mixed to say the least — David Bradley is probably the standout, but what he has to work with prevents him from excelling any further; beyond him, I am not remotely impressed. Ewan McGregor, Tilda Swinton, Christoph Waltz and Burn Gorman are all capable of truly exceptional work — but here they are all wasted; and why bother casting someone as skilled as Cate Blanchett in a role that anyone could have played? As for the central child performance, I’m not a fan either — no disrespect to Gregory Mann, who I hope has a long and prosperous career ahead of him, but I find him grating and offputting in the role, with most of his delivery being stilted and inorganic. Overall, an all-star cast squandered. I’m well aware of the unpopularity of this opinion, and it’s not like there’s nothing redemptive here — the animators are obviously master craftsmen who should be commended for their massive efforts, and I appreciate this adaptation taking risks and trying something new with the classic story (though it does amuse me that, even when set in fascist Italy and focussing on the inevitability of mortal expiration, this version is not even remotely close to being as fucked up as the original). I love the concept of Pinocchio having the embodiment of death as a mentor figure, but this — like the other interesting ideas — is never expanded upon in any meaningful way. Plus, the stakes are completely compromised, and goalposts are constantly moved; several frustrating deus-ex-machina moments — like the avatars constantly bending or breaking their own rules and impossible feats being brushed over — prevent me ever taking the characters’ plights seriously. To me, this is an assortment of potentially brilliant individual pieces that can’t form a satisfying whole, with the disparity between the surface-level whimsy and the profoundly unremarkable tedium of the actual content being wider than The Terrible Dogfish’s maw. I totally understand those who extol the former element, but I just don’t meaningfully resonate with anything else.

Guillermo del Toro's Veggie Tales It's interesting to read the synopsis for Collodi's original story in order to see why GDT didn't just render it faithfully. In that version, Geppetto creates Pinnochio in hopes of teaching him to entertain and thus earn a living. Pinnochio rejects his authority first and foremost, and he kills Jimminy Cricket unceremoniously on his way out the door. It's the Disney movie that imparts the story with sentimentality. It's the Disney movie that puts together big musical sequences. Where GDT adheres to Collodi's vision is in making his adaptation instructive. Instead of teaching Pinnochio how to be a proper and productive Italian citizen however, he critiques the forces seeking to exploit him. His take on the picaresque fairy tale is full of obvious biblical allegory critiquing the church, the state, and labor exploitation. These are all things GDT has done before and done better. So what claims to be one man's vision is the work of  Collodi, Walt Disney, and God as well. There's a co-director and a cowriter to consider. This is a lovingly animated hodgepodge, but it's a hodgepodge nonetheless. Too many cooks.

A revisit and reappraisal of this film was not kind to it, for me. I rewatched most of Del Toro’s Pinocchio recently (can’t remember exact date so I’m estimating), mostly out of curiosity over how the film had gotten so much worse in my mind. In talking about it to a friend, I realized I didn’t like it anymore, whereas my initial viewing had left me mostly fond of it though equally baffled by it. Turns out, I don’t really like this movie. It always feels reductive to call a film boring, but I found myself uninterested in large segments of this film’s runtime. The animation is always impressive, in addition to being downright off-putting, and many of the character depictions and designs do a lot to magnify that off-putting sense. The messaging is painfully on-the-nose and heavy handed, even if it’s genuinely interesting here and there because, damn, it isn’t afraid to go to some dark places. And the songs? I hate the songs. I hate them so much. That Mussolini poop song? I’ll say I’m glad it exists, but that’s all, because how funny is it to say to somebody: “Oh, Guillermo Del Toro’s Pinocchio? The story itself offers little in the way of a fresh twist, but as a work of art, the stop-motion animation is impressive. Making full use of the latest technology while still adhering to the fundamental rules of stop-motion, the film creates visuals that retain a sense of simplicity while feeling fresh and never becoming tiresome to look at. Its central message is that it is okay to remain who you are, even if you are different from everyone else. I was particularly moved by the ultimate expression of that idea: continuing to live even after everyone you love has left. There is the loneliness that comes from loving and being loved as oneself, and the loneliness that comes from not being able to do so. Perhaps the former is the deeper kind of loneliness, even if it ultimately has more meaning than the empty loneliness of the latter. Whatever path we choose, the film reminded me once again that there is no escaping loneliness as a human being.

“Terrible, terrible joy.” Finn Wolfhard trying to be British… Ariana what are you doing here? First off, let me shower the visuals with praise. I adore stop motion and it’s such a good medium with which to tell a puppet’s story. The locations are beautiful and filled with personality, I love the designs of the characters so much. Inside the Whale looks especially impressively gross, but my favourite sequences of the whole movie are the ones in the afterlife with the Blue Fairy, who has a killer design. The hourglasses and the lighting and the hares bantering over cards all feel like they were engineered to appeal to me specifically. So so so cool. Also, using Pinocchio to explore father/son relationships and then how that intersects with the state, especially during Mussolini’s Italy is just such a creative concept and I love it. I do have a few complaints that hold this one back for me. I found it a little irritating until maybe Pinocchio’s first death scene - after that it kicked into gear and I liked it a bit more. It didn’t help that at first Pinocchio was an utter menace, causing more damage than The Cat in the Hat . Like obviously I do not agree with the fascists but they were right Pinocchio needs to lock the fuck in. A lot of the characters kind of grated on me, but they got better after that. The dialogue the whole way through felt a little clunky though. The themes are presented well enough on their own, you don’t need to explain them!!!! As much as I love musicals, I found the songs irritating because the scansion was off and they were all too short to really get a sense of their purpose. Don’t make a musical if you’re not going to fully commit to it!! Criminal that the best song in the movie is saved only for the end credits. Desplat still kills it with the orchestral stuff though, no surprises there. It’s no Pinocchio: A True Story , but it ain’t half bad. Also this would go crazy as a Next to Normal AU.

Never wrote this at the couple of times that I’ve watched this movie, but my god every time I watch this I bawl my eyes out. As a person who cries happy tears mostly, I can’t even express how strong emotions I’ve felt during this absolute masterpiece.

Gillermo del Toro has a very nakedly sincere approach to storytelling, its hard not to love him when he expresses this sincerity and passion for life itself in his movies. Pinnochio, both the interpetation of the character and the movie as a whole, is brimming with this infectious love of life, its transparently clear how much talent and effort went into expressing the beauty of fascination with what surrounds us. It was such a lucid decsion to make this with stop motion, to choose an approach that doesnt try to make the author invisible, but the opposite; the whole time you can tell that these are real, delicately crafted objects that somebody took the time to bring life to them, to build them with care and painstakingly animate them, it highlights their efforts without being obtrusive, giving space for the work to breathe. In an age where creativity and imagination are trying to be either buried under the veneer of disinterest or unimportance or commodified for profit, to see something so honest, so loving, so sweet, so kind to the human spirit is to witness a miracle.
